whyCorrect: Only the tiles that were taken off matter first: 480 - 165 = 315 tiles left the pallet. Those 315 tiles came off in 7 equal loads, so each load held 315 ÷ 7 = 45 tiles. You can check it: 7(45) = 315, and 480 - 315 = 165.

whyWrong.A: 35 leaves too many tiles behind: 7(35) = 245 removed, so 480 - 245 = 235 would remain, not 165. It is what you get by dividing 315 by 9 instead of by 7.
whyWrong.C: 55 removes 7(55) = 385 tiles, leaving only 95 on the pallet.
whyWrong.D: 63 is 315 ÷ 5, not 315 ÷ 7 — it divides the removed tiles by the wrong number of loads. Seven loads of 63 would strip 441 tiles off a pallet that only held 480.

commonMistakes: Dividing 480 by 7 instead of first subtracting the 165 tiles that were never taken off.
tips: In a "take away equal amounts" problem, find the total removed before you divide.

whyCorrect: The 8 kilograms of crate are there whether or not tiles are in it, so subtract that first: 71 - 8 = 63 kilograms of tiles. Each tile is 3 kilograms, so there are 63 ÷ 3 = 21 tiles. As an equation, 3n + 8 = 71 gives 3n = 63 and n = 21.

whyWrong.B: 23 comes from dividing 71 by 3 and rounding down — it ignores the crate's own 8 kilograms. Check it: 3(23) + 8 = 77, not 71.
whyWrong.C: 24 is 71 ÷ 3 rounded up, again with the crate mass left in. 3(24) + 8 = 80 kilograms.
whyWrong.D: 26 comes from adding the crate mass instead of subtracting it: (71 + 8) ÷ 3 ≈ 26. The crate mass has to come off the total before you divide.

commonMistakes: Dividing the full 71 kilograms by 3 without removing the fixed mass of the empty crate.
tips: Write the situation as one equation, 3n + 8 = 71, and the order of operations takes care of itself.

whyCorrect: A linear function changes by the same amount over equal steps in x. Each 2-unit step here adds 6 to the output: 11 to 17 to 23. Since x = 8 is one more 2-unit step past x = 6, h(8) = 23 + 6 = 29. In rule form the slope is 6 ÷ 2 = 3 and the constant is 11 - 3(2) = 5, so h(x) = 3x + 5 and h(8) = 29.

whyWrong.A: 26 adds the per-unit rate of 3 just once. From x = 6 to x = 8 is two units, so you must add 3 twice, or 6 in total.
whyWrong.B: 27 is the value of the rule 3x + 3. The constant is 5, not 3, because 11 - 3(2) = 5.
whyWrong.D: 31 adds 8 — the x-value itself — to h(6) = 23. What gets added is the change in output over the step, which is 6.

commonMistakes: Confusing the step in x (2) with the step in h (6).
tips: Check any linear rule you build against every row of the table, not just the one you used to find it.

whyCorrect: Constant speed means rate = change in height ÷ change in time, and both changes must come from the same pair of readings. The height goes from 9 metres to 21 metres, a rise of 12 metres, while the time goes from 2 seconds to 6 seconds, a gap of 4 seconds. So the rate is 12 ÷ 4 = 3 metres per second.

whyWrong.A: At 1 metre per second the load would rise only 4 metres in the 4 seconds between the two readings, but it rises 12.
whyWrong.B: 2 comes from dividing the 12-metre rise by 6 — the later time — instead of by the 4-second gap between the readings. At 2 metres per second the rise would be 8 metres.
whyWrong.C: 2.5 metres per second gives a rise of 2.5(4) = 10 metres between the readings, not 12.

commonMistakes: Dividing a height by a clock time instead of dividing the change in height by the change in time.
tips: Test any rate you find by multiplying it back through the time gap and comparing with the given rise.

whyCorrect: You need 22n > 300, so n > 300 ÷ 22 ≈ 13.6. The number of stones is a whole number, so the least value that works is 14: 22(14) = $308, which is more than $300.

whyWrong.A: 13 stones pay 22(13) = $286, which is less than $300. Rounding 13.6 down goes the wrong way when the inequality is "more than".
whyWrong.C: 15 stones do pay more than $300, but $330 is not the least such pay — 14 stones already clear $300.
whyWrong.D: 16 stones also clear $300 at $352, but the question asks for the smallest number that does, not just any number that does.

commonMistakes: Rounding 13.6 down to 13 out of habit; when you need to exceed a target, you round up.
tips: After dividing, always multiply your candidate back and check it really passes the "more than" test.

whyCorrect: Collect the x terms on one side and the numbers on the other. Subtracting 4x from both sides gives 3x - 12 = 27, and adding 12 to both sides gives 3x = 39, so x = 13. Check: 7(13) - 12 = 79 and 4(13) + 27 = 79.

whyWrong.A: 5 comes from subtracting 12 from 27 instead of adding it, giving 3x = 15. The -12 is on the left, so it moves across as +12.
whyWrong.B: 9 comes from dropping the -12 entirely and solving 3x = 27. Substituting back gives 51 on the left and 63 on the right.
whyWrong.D: 15 does not balance the equation: 7(15) - 12 = 93 while 4(15) + 27 = 87.

commonMistakes: Moving a term across the equals sign without changing its sign.
tips: Substitute your answer into both sides — a linear equation has one solution, so a single check settles it.

whyCorrect: Subtract 8 from both sides of \(5x+8\le 78\) to get \(5x\le 70\) , then divide by 5 to get \(x\le 14\) . Since x must be a whole number of tiles and 14 itself satisfies the inequality, the greatest number is 14.

whyWrong.B: 15 comes from ignoring the +8 and computing 78 ÷ 5 = 15.6, then rounding down. With the 8 included, 5(15) + 8 = 83, which is more than 78.
whyWrong.C: 16 gives 5(16) + 8 = 88 tiles' worth of load, well over the limit of 78.
whyWrong.D: 17 gives 5(17) + 8 = 93, further over the limit. Once x exceeds 14 the inequality fails.

commonMistakes: Rounding up after dividing; for a "no more than" limit you round down to stay under it.
tips: Solve the inequality fully, then test the whole number you land on in the original inequality.

whyCorrect: You do not need a or b separately. Notice that 6a + 9b = 3(2a + 3b), because 3(2a) = 6a and 3(3b) = 9b. Since 2a + 3b = 17, the value is 3(17) = 51.

whyWrong.A: 17 is the value of 2a + 3b itself. The expression asked about is three times that, not the same as it.
whyWrong.B: 34 is 2(17), which would be the value of 4a + 6b. Check the multiplier: 6a is three times 2a, not twice it.

commonMistakes: Trying to solve for a and b individually — one equation in two unknowns has no single solution, which is the hint that a multiple is wanted.
tips: When a question gives one equation in two variables, look for the target expression as a constant multiple of the one you were given.

whyCorrect: Expand the expression and match it term by term with ax + 8. Distributing the -2 gives 7x - 2x + 8, which collects to 5x + 8. Comparing with ax + 8, the coefficient of x is a = 5.

whyWrong.A: 3 comes from subtracting the 2 twice — once from 7x and once again — instead of just once. Only 2x is taken away, leaving 5x.
whyWrong.C: 7 leaves the -2(x) undistributed, keeping 7x and picking up only the +8. The -2 multiplies both terms inside the parentheses.
whyWrong.D: 9 comes from adding 2x rather than subtracting it. The sign in front of the parentheses is negative, so 7x - 2x = 5x.

commonMistakes: Distributing the -2 onto the -4 but forgetting it also multiplies the x.
tips: Expand first, collect like terms, and only then compare coefficients with the target form.

whyCorrect: A product is zero exactly when one of its factors is zero, so set each factor to zero separately. From x - 2 = 0 you get x = 2, and from x + 6 = 0 you get x = -6. So \(h(x)=0\) at x = -6 and x = 2.

whyWrong.A: -6 and -2 negates both numbers. The factor x - 2 is zero when x is +2, not -2, since 2 - 2 = 0.
whyWrong.C: -2 and 6 has both signs flipped the wrong way round: it solves x + 2 = 0 and x - 6 = 0, which are not the factors given.
whyWrong.D: 2 and 6 reads the numbers straight out of the factors without changing sign. Check it: h(6) = (4)(12) = 48, not 0.

commonMistakes: Copying the constants out of the factors instead of solving each factor for zero.
tips: Substitute each value back into the original product — a zero has to make one factor vanish.

whyCorrect: You need the value of x with \(x^{2}=196\) , which is the square root of 196. Since 14 × 14 = 196, there are 14 tiles along each side. A side length must be positive, so the negative root is not a possible count.

whyWrong.C: 16 gives \(16^{2}=256\) tiles, more than the stack holds.
whyWrong.D: 98 is 196 ÷ 2. Halving finds the side of a rectangle two tiles deep, not the side of a square; squaring 98 gives 9,604.

commonMistakes: Dividing by 2 instead of taking a square root.
tips: Multiply your candidate by itself and compare with the given total — squaring is faster than rooting to check.

whyCorrect: In \(p(n)\) the input n is the number of tiles and the output is the price in dollars. So \(p(40)=70\) says that when 40 tiles are bought, the price is $70. Check it against the rule: 1.75(40) = 70.

whyWrong.A: This treats the input 40 as a price. 40 is a number of tiles; the price of one tile is the 1.75 in the rule.
whyWrong.B: This swaps the input and the output. 70 is the dollar amount, not a count of tiles.
whyWrong.C: $70 is the price of all 40 tiles together, not the price of one. One tile costs $1.75.

commonMistakes: Reading the number inside the parentheses as the answer rather than as the input.
tips: Name the units of the input and the output before you read any function statement.

whyCorrect: On the graph of y = f(x), the horizontal coordinate is the input x and the vertical coordinate is the output f(x). Since \(f(6)=19\) , the input 6 pairs with the output 19, giving the point (6, 19).

whyWrong.A: (0, 19) puts the output in the right place but claims the input is 0, which the statement says nothing about.
whyWrong.B: (19, 0) reverses the coordinates and then sets the output to 0. Nothing given says the hoist takes 0 minutes for anything.
whyWrong.C: (19, 6) has the two numbers the wrong way round — it would mean 19 crates take 6 minutes.

commonMistakes: Writing the output first because it appears on the right of the equals sign.
tips: Read \(f(6)=19\) as "input 6, output 19" and the ordered pair writes itself.

whyCorrect: "One quarter of the plain tiles" means one quarter of the two thirds, so you multiply the fractions rather than combining them any other way: \(\frac{2}{3}\times\frac{1}{4}=\frac{2}{12}=\frac{1}{6}\) . A concrete check: with 120 tiles, 80 are plain and a quarter of those, 20, are seconds, and 20 out of 120 is \(\frac{1}{6}\) .

whyWrong.A: \(\frac{1}{12}\) is \(\frac{1}{3}\times\frac{1}{4}\) — it uses one third of the pallet as plain instead of two thirds.
whyWrong.B: \(\frac{1}{8}\) is a quarter of one half. The plain tiles are two thirds of the pallet, not half of it.
whyWrong.D: \(\frac{5}{12}\) is \(\frac{2}{3}-\frac{1}{4}\) . The word "of" signals multiplication here, not subtraction.

commonMistakes: Adding or subtracting the two fractions because both describe the same pallet.
tips: When one fraction is taken "of" another, multiply — and test with a convenient total such as 120.

whyCorrect: A fraction of the whole pallet needs the whole pallet in the denominator, so add all four rows: 180 + 96 + 72 + 12 = 360 tiles. The ridge tiles are 72 of those, and \(\frac{72}{360}=\frac{1}{5}\) .

whyWrong.C: \(\frac{1}{6}\) of 360 is 60 tiles. You would get this fraction only if the total were 432 — a sign a row was added twice or misread.

commonMistakes: Leaving one row out of the total, which changes the denominator and every candidate fraction with it.
tips: Multiply each answer choice by your total; the one that returns the row's own count is the fraction you want.

whyCorrect: "How many times" asks for the ratio of the two counts, so divide the plain tiles by the ridge tiles: 480 ÷ 120 = 4. Check it by multiplying back: 4(120) = 480.

whyWrong.A: 2 would mean there are 2(120) = 240 plain tiles on the pallet.
whyWrong.B: 3 is (480 - 120) ÷ 120, which answers how many times more numerous the plain tiles are, not how many times as numerous.
whyWrong.D: 5 is the total of both kinds, 600, divided by 120. The question compares plain tiles with ridge tiles, not the whole pallet with the ridge tiles.

commonMistakes: Dividing the pallet total by one part instead of dividing one part by the other.
tips: After dividing, multiply your answer by the smaller count and confirm you get the larger one back.

whyCorrect: "Recorded on more of those days than any other" is asking for the value that appears most often — the mode. Counting the list 4, 2, 5, 2, 6, 2, 7, the number 2 appears three times and every other number appears once. So the answer is 2.

whyWrong.B: 4 is the mean of the list (the seven values total 28, and 28 ÷ 7 = 4) and also the median, but it was recorded on only one day.
whyWrong.C: 5 appears on just one of the seven days.
whyWrong.D: 7 is the largest number of breakages, not the most frequent one; it too appears once.

commonMistakes: Reporting the mean or the largest value when the question asks which value occurred most often.
tips: Sort or tally the list before you answer; the repeated value is then impossible to miss.

whyCorrect: One complete turn of the drum unwinds a length of rope equal to the drum's circumference, and the load rises by that much. The circumference is \(2\pi r=2\pi(25)=50\pi\) centimetres.

whyWrong.A: \(25\pi\) is \(\pi r\) — half the circumference. The formula uses twice the radius, since the diameter is 50.
whyWrong.B: \(35\pi\) is the circumference of a drum of diameter 35 centimetres. Here the diameter is 2(25) = 50.
whyWrong.D: \(625\pi\) is \(\pi r^{2}\) , the drum's cross-sectional area in square centimetres. Rope length is a distance, so it comes from the circumference.

commonMistakes: Reaching for the area formula because a circle is involved; a distance travelled per turn is a circumference.
tips: Check the units in your head — an answer in centimetres cannot come from squaring a length.

whyCorrect: The angle sits at the peg, so the mast height 15 is the opposite side and the ground distance is the adjacent side. Since \(\tan\) equals opposite over adjacent, \(\frac{15}{d}=\frac{5}{2}\) . Cross-multiplying gives 5d = 30, so d = 6 metres.

whyWrong.B: 7.5 is 15 ÷ 2, using only the bottom number of the ratio. Both numbers of \(\frac{5}{2}\) have to be used.
whyWrong.C: 12 does not satisfy the ratio: 15 ÷ 12 = 1.25, not 2.5. It comes from treating 15 as the rope's length and reading off a 9-12-15 triangle, but 15 is the vertical side, not the rope.
whyWrong.D: 37.5 is 15 multiplied by \(\frac{5}{2}\) instead of divided by it. Since the tangent is greater than 1, the adjacent side must be shorter than 15, not longer.

commonMistakes: Putting the unknown on top when the unknown is the adjacent side.
tips: Write the ratio with the known height in the numerator first, then solve — it keeps the multiply-or-divide decision from being a guess.

whyCorrect: Find the mean first: 12 + 9 + 15 + 8 + 20 + 14 + 6 = 84, and 84 ÷ 7 = 12. Now compare each figure with 12. The values above 12 are 15, 20 and 14 — that is 3 of them. (The 12 itself is not greater than the mean, so it does not count.)
commonMistakes: Counting the value that equals the mean; "greater than" excludes it.
tips: Add the list once, divide by how many values there are, then run down the list ticking off the ones above that number.

whyCorrect: "Measures 42 centimetres across" gives the diameter, so the radius is 42 ÷ 2 = 21 centimetres. The area is \(\pi r^{2}=\pi(21)^{2}=441\pi\) square centimetres, so k = 441.
commonMistakes: Squaring the 42 instead of the radius, which gives 1,764 — the across-measurement of a circle is its diameter, not its radius.
tips: Halve the diameter before you square, never after.

whyCorrect: Two angles that together make a straight line are supplementary, so they add to 180°. That gives (3x + 20) + (2x - 5) = 180. Collecting terms, 5x + 15 = 180, so 5x = 165 and x = 33. Check: the angles are 119° and 61°, which add to 180°.
commonMistakes: Setting the two expressions equal to each other, which would only be right if the angles were stated to be equal, or using 90° instead of 180°.
tips: "Together make a straight line" is always the signal for a sum of 180 degrees.

whyCorrect: You do not need x and y separately. Factor the difference of squares: \(x^{2}-y^{2}=(x+y)(x-y)\) . Substituting the first equation gives \(13(x-y)=91\) , so \(x-y=91\div 13=7\) .

whyWrong.A: 3 is the value of y, not of \(x-y\) . Solving the pair gives x = 10 and y = 3, so it is the right number read off the wrong variable.
whyWrong.C: 13 is the value of \(x+y\) , which was given. The two sums are not the same: 10 + 3 = 13 but 10 - 3 = 7.
whyWrong.D: 91 is the value of \(x^{2}-y^{2}\) . That is 13 times the quantity asked for, because the difference of squares carries the factor \(x+y\) .

commonMistakes: Trying to solve the quadratic system term by term instead of spotting the difference-of-squares factoring.
tips: Whenever you see \(x^{2}-y^{2}\) beside \(x+y\) or \(x-y\) , factor first — the given sum divides straight out.

whyCorrect: Split the 32 stones at the point where the rate changes. The first 20 pay d each, for 20d. The remaining 32 - 20 = 12 stones pay half of d each, for \(12\left(\frac{d}{2}\right)=6d\) . The total is 20d + 6d = 26d.

whyWrong.B: 28d makes the extra 12 stones worth 8d, a rate of \(\frac{2d}{3}\) each rather than the stated half rate.
whyWrong.C: 30d makes the extra 12 stones worth 10d. Half of d is \(\frac{d}{2}\) , so 12 of them come to 6d, not 10d.
whyWrong.D: 32d pays the full rate d for all 32 stones and ignores the reduced rate entirely.

commonMistakes: Halving the number of extra stones and the rate, or forgetting that only the stones past the 20th are paid at the lower rate.
tips: Write two products — full rate times 20, half rate times the remainder — and add them; never apply one rate to the whole amount.
